explain.say: Blow on hot soup and it cools faster. Your breath carries the heat away. Heat moving with a flowing fluid is convection. Look at a computer chip: it passes heat into a finned heat sink, and a fan blows air across the fins to carry it off.

draw.text: Convection = conduction into a fluid + the fluid moving away

explain.say: Newton's law of cooling says the heat flow Q equals h times A times the difference between the surface and the fluid temperature. Here h is the heat transfer coefficient, how good the flow is at carrying heat. With fan air, h is about 50. The sink has 0.05 square metres at 40 degrees above the air: Q is 100 watts.

explain.say: Natural convection is when warm air simply rises by itself. Forced convection is when a fan or pump drives the flow. See the bars? Still air gives h around 10, a fan about 100, pumped water thousands, boiling water tens of thousands. So switch the fan off and what happens to the chip?

draw.text: Typical h values; real ones vary a lot with speed and shape

explain.say: It heats up until the bigger temperature difference pushes the same 100 watts out. Now the graph: a coffee cooling in a room. The rate of cooling is proportional to how much hotter it is than the room, so it falls fast at first, then slowly. It starts at 90 degrees and reaches about 46 after 15 minutes.

faq.q: How does a heat sink get rid of heat?
faq.a: Heat conducts from the chip into the metal sink and spreads into its fins. Air flowing over the fins then carries it away by convection.
asks: how does a CPU cooler work

faq.q: Why does a fan cool things faster?
faq.a: Moving air sweeps warm air away from the surface and thins the slow boundary layer, which raises the heat transfer coefficient h.

faq.q: What does Newton's cooling curve look like?
faq.a: The temperature falls exponentially towards the surroundings: fast at first when the difference is big, then slower and slower.

faq.q: What is Newton's law of cooling?
faq.a: The convective heat flow equals h times area times the temperature difference between the surface and the fluid far away.

faq.q: What is the convective heat transfer coefficient?
faq.a: h, in watts per square metre kelvin, measures how well a fluid flow carries heat from a surface. It depends on the fluid, its speed and the geometry.

facts: Natural convection in air gives h of about 2 to 25 W/m²·K; forced air about 25 to 250.
Boiling and condensation give some of the highest heat transfer coefficients of all.
